summary: Docusate (docusate sodium or docusate calcium) is an emollient, surfactant-type stool softener used to relieve occasional constipation and to prevent straining (for example after surgery, myocardial infarction or in haemorrhoids). It is an anionic surfactant that reduces the surface tension of stool, letting water and fats penetrate and soften the faecal mass; it generally produces a bowel movement in 12 to 72 hours. The usual adult oral dose of docusate sodium is 100 mg one to three times daily (commonly 100-300 mg/day, with up to 500 mg/day used). It is well tolerated with little systemic absorption. It should not be used with mineral oil (it can increase mineral-oil absorption) and should not be taken if there is abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, a recent marked change in bowel habit lasting over two weeks, or rectal bleeding without medical advice. If a stool softener is needed for more than one week, or there is no bowel movement after use, a doctor should be consulted.
indications: Prevention of straining at stool where this is undesirable (e.g. after surgery or myocardial infarction, anorectal conditions, haemorrhoids)

moa: Docusate is an anionic surfactant (wetting agent). It lowers the surface tension at the oil-water interface of the stool, allowing intestinal water and lipids to penetrate and mix with the faecal mass, which softens the stool and eases passage. It is classed as an emollient/softener laxative rather than a stimulant and works gradually over 12 to 72 hours; it has little or no direct stimulant effect on intestinal motility.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to docusate or formulation components
relative: Acute abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting of unknown cause
Sudden change in bowel habit lasting over 2 weeks
monitor: Need for continued use beyond 1 week (reassess for underlying cause)

preg: Docusate has minimal systemic absorption and is generally considered low risk and acceptable for occasional use in pregnancy, but pregnant women should ask a health professional before use, as constipation in pregnancy is often managed first with fluids, fibre and bulk-forming agents.
lact: Because of negligible systemic absorption, docusate is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding. Ask a health professional before regular use.
renal: No dose adjustment is required; docusate is minimally absorbed and acts locally in the gut.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is needed. Avoid combining with mineral oil, as docusate may enhance the absorption of mineral oil, and use cautiously where hepatic concerns exist.

moderate: Mineral oil - docusate may increase systemic absorption of mineral oil; avoid concurrent use
minor: May theoretically enhance absorption of other co-administered drugs by its surfactant action
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; take with adequate fluid
interactions.diagnostics: No clinically significant effects on laboratory tests

serious: Rarely, throat irritation with liquid preparations
rare: Electrolyte disturbance with prolonged excessive use
emergency: Signs of bowel obstruction (severe pain, persistent vomiting, no passage of stool or gas)

monitoring: Bowel movement frequency and stool consistency
Resolution of constipation within the expected 12-72 hours
Reassessment if a laxative is needed for more than one week
counsel: This medicine softens the stool to make it easier to pass; it may take 1 to 3 days to work
Drink plenty of fluids and eat fibre to help it work and prevent constipation returning
Do not use it with mineral oil unless your doctor tells you to
Do not use for more than a week without medical advice, and stop if you have rectal bleeding or no bowel movement
Tell a doctor before use if you have stomach pain, nausea, vomiting or a recent marked change in bowel habit
Keep out of reach of children and seek help in case of overdose

Acts locally in the gut; minimal systemic absorption

pearls: Stool softener, not a stimulant - best for preventing straining and softening hard stools, not for rapid relief
Onset is slow (12-72 h); little evidence of efficacy for established or chronic constipation
Do not combine with mineral oil (increases mineral-oil absorption)
Minimal systemic absorption - generally safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding for occasional use
Maintain hydration and fibre intake for the softener to work effectively
Persistent need beyond a week warrants evaluation for an underlying cause
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember, or skip it if it is almost time for the next dose - do not take a double dose. Docusate is taken as needed for constipation, so an occasional missed dose is not a problem.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely to be serious; excessive use may cause abdominal cramping and diarrhoea, with potential fluid and electrolyte loss on prolonged misuse. Treatment is supportive with fluid and electrolyte replacement; contact a Poison Control Center for guidance.
